Well Miles as a person if you look at his career, he would go through a period, like he had the small band quintet, then he went through the Gil Evans period with large orchestras, then he went into more funk type quintet's later on and then you know into the Coltrane era and all that kind of thing and then got into the Bitches Brew period and in other words Miles never liked to repeat himself or do anything. But finally towards the end of his life even though we didn't realize it he was starting to – Quincy kept bugging him about this ‘cause it was gonna be on Qwest and wanted to get Miles to – you know and Miles just never liked to look back, he wasn't that kind of a guy and that's why he shied away from doing things he had done before not because he didn't think there were valid he just liked doing new things. He was similar to Gil that way, to Gil Evans.
Now did you talk with Miles directly about this project.
Really only had one conversation, it was over the phone, but we agreed, we wanted to do it.
When was this around 1990 or so?
Yeah, right about.
Oh, that’s…
I really wished we had done it.
That's tragic that that didn't happen.
Well it is, but it didn't happen, so you know.
An unfair but interesting question, what kind of instrumentation do you think would you have used, would you use strings, what would you have used?

It would have been dictated by what kind of material we did, what I wrote and all that. That would have dictated it. Yeah, chances are I would have used strings, might have used a similar type of instrumentation to what I used in The Sandpiper, or possibly on the Sanborn [David] album [Pearls] but it would have been a totally different kind of album. Probably a lot more esoteric, I’m not sure where it would have gone, which is why I can’t say what instruments I’d have used. It’s too early in the game when you don’t even have your material to try and decide what kind of a setting you’re gonna use for it.
Of course. Well speaking of The Sandpiper, why don’t we jump back to say the early 60s.
Yes.
Alright.
Or, in fairness that you said after you’d done, I Want to Live! you had done TV writing you had done a couple of, B movies.
I did a lot of vocal albums.
And we’ve discussed those.

And really… then did the Andy Williams, I was gonna say Andy Warhol, Andy Williams and right after the Andy Williams thing, I really got connected up with Filmways [Production Company] and got a shot to do The Americanization of Emily, a very good picture, a

chance to write a song, something I hadn't foreseen. And my first song of any consequence, even though when I look back now I had written songs that could've been songs. But I never thought of myself as a songwriter.
“Just a Child,” goes under that category doesn’t it?
Yeah, and stuff from, I Want to Live!, “Barbara’s theme,” you know several themes in that could've taken lyrics.
Oh, that reminds me…
“Black Nightgown,” a lot of those could’ve taken lyrics.
Three of those tunes, “Barbara’s Theme,” and, “Black Nightgown,” and the theme from, I Want to Live! you did charts for Gerry Mulligan on.
Yeah.
That Mulligan recorded with a concert jazz band.
Yeah, I think so, right, yeah.
So he basically, he just called you and said I like all these tunes that I played on the score or heard on the score and I’d like you to do charts for my band?
Yeah, it was it, and I was around New York at that time, so I went and rehearsed the band and all that stuff.
Apparently he brought Holman east to work in New York…
That’s right; Bill was with us at the same time.
So you just did those three charts then? You didn’t do anything else?
Yeah, that’s all ‘cause I’d left New York after that, went back home to California.
But he recorded all three of them.
Um-hm.
And they all sounded terrific.
Great, well with those players, good God, you could’ve written stuff that wasn't very good and it would've sounded terrific.
Yeah, Stan Getz later recorded, “Barbara's Theme.”
That’s another thing I didn’t know, you have to watch Stan Getz at all times or he’s libel to record something of yours.
[They both laugh]
Have you heard that record?
No, I haven't.
It’s going to be reissued shortly; it was on an album called, Voices, that was done with a rhythm section with Herbie Hancock and Ron Carter and Grady Tate.
Oh, I’d like to have heard that combination.
And a chorus with Claus Ogerman arrangements.
I’d really like to have heard that, a chorus and Claus plus strings?
No, no strings, just a chorus and rhythm section.

No its…

Oh, oh, well, you know…

Oh yeah…
“I Didn’t Know What Time it Was.”

Yeah.

Yes.

That was an album we made in 1955 called, Rain or Shine, and it was really one of the only good albums being made except the Sinatra albums and maybe the Farnon Albums, that I knew of, probably there were others. He’s one of a kind…

So, say if we were to discuss…
You can’t compare him to Robert Farnon.
It’s definitely apples and oranges.
You can’t compare anyone to Robert Farnon. Robert Farnon is simply the best.
What do you hear in Farnon’s work that particularly appeals to you?
Everything I’ve stolen.
[laughs loud] You don’t mind if I tell Gene Lees these lines, he’s – I think he actually might have mailed, he did a three part jazz letter on Robert Farnon…
Well then you’ll read that in there…
Oh, okay.

[laughs]

How about Marion Evans?
Great arranger, I’m sorry he gave up music.

He’s the one that showed us all how.

He makes strings sound like they always should have sounded. He knows how to wrench at me, I personally respond a great deal to what he does, his choices of everything, his harmonic choices. I can only speak of my own experience, I don’t know about what the other writers hear, but they probably hear the same things I like.
I would say so.
It’s a none-sensational approach, it’s totally the opposite of Michel’s, he never goes for shock or for effect.
I was going to use the word, “sober,” to describe him as opposed to Michel’s which is as you call it, “flashy.”

Yeah, most people didn't really realize how great Alex North was, you listen to Cleopatra, Whose Afraid of Virginia Woolf or Spartacus or any one of them they’re just, they are masterpieces. And his orchestration is all like fine line drawing, he really knew his orchestra to.

He may have, yeah.

Sure.

I remember reading…

Only peripherally.
About songs?
I want to get to that definitely.
Oh, all right then…

I was starting to say about Emily getting back to that, that was the first time I had like a really good fat string section from MGM, the MGM staff string section and a wonderful soundstage, the MGM soundstage of that time which was 1963, ‘64. And oh boy, you know when I started hearing all those sounds coming out, it was like all that time I had spent trying to make those sounds kind of finally paid off, I never realized that I'd have that kind of an opportunity. Where you have all those violins on a note, instead of just a couple of them and the stuff really sounded like you’d envisioned it. So it was wonderful being able to do that movie and people liked it which I liked too, you know the people I worked for. Which in movies is a really nice thing to have happen because often it doesn't go that way ‘cause there are some very flaky people making movies, these days and even in those days that know nothing about music but they all think they do. And then after that I had a chance for the same producers to do The Sandpiper, and I used much more of a jazz type of approach for that. With kind of an extended large big-band kind of sound with strings, you know but with all the woodwinds and you know colors, I was able to go for colors because we were scoring a lot of exteriors of Big Sur and all the – you know it was a gorgeous picture visually so there were all kinds of things to go off of when I was writing.

Sure did…
Solo voice.

Yes it was, it was originally instrumental theme and then we got…
It was, “Love Theme from The Sandpiper,” right?
Um-hm.

He’s right, all I wrote was [sings melody of “The Shadow of Your Smile”]
[they both laugh]

Oh really?
And he had every, yeah, and he had every reason to be irate. It was like the old story with…
Oscar Hammerstein’s wife?
Oscar Hammerstein and, “Ol’ Man River,” Jerome Kerns, “Ol’ Man River,” and Dorothy Hammerstein got furious she said, “Mr. Kern wrote da-da-dada, Oscar wrote, “Ol’ Man River.””
[they both laugh]

Yeah, look…
And through the ages they have, Gershwin’s it’s always George it's never Ira and Ira was invaluable to George, as great as George was and believe me he was great.
Johnny Mercer might be the only exception because I've heard tunes referred to as Johnny Mercer tunes that were tunes where he actually wrote the lyric but not the music.
And he wrote wonderful music when he wrote it. All of Johnny Mercer's music that he ever wrote was very good, as musical and natural as could be. I love his songs when he wrote both.
Yeah, a little later on I have a whole list of lyricists that you’ve associated with…
Okay.
That I want to just talk with you about. So, “Shadow of Your Smile,” won the Academy award that year.
It sure did.

No. It wasn’t that it wasn’t a surprise it was just by the time the Academy campaigns and everything heated up, you know winning an Academy Award is pretty much like running for office, to be perfectly honest. That doesn’t mean to imply that there’s anything fixed about the voting, there isn’t, but in order to get your product—your product, --in order to get yourself heard and people be aware of who wrote what, you had to take adds, you had to go on shows, you had to do all those things. And you’d hire a publicist quite frankly and everyone did it, Mancini would do it, whoever was – you know had a song or a score that was in contention that had made the nominations. So, I didn’t know it was going to win but I knew it had a very good chance. I had no idea it was really going to win and I was very delighted when it did, you never

really know about the Oscars until the last minute. You can tell by the people, that’s not acting, they’re not giving academy award performances at the Oscars when they pretend to go into shock, they really are going into shock.
So what did this award do for you in terms of, I don’t know, what’s the term, credibility, visibility, how did it – did it enhance your career?

No, it did not. The phone stopped ringing for the strangest reason. It was very bizarre and to this day I’ll never know why, but I had a lot of work stacked up before that, so I did a number of pictures after it until they all ran out. But no, winning the Academy Award didn’t hurt me but it sure never helped. And why it didn’t, I’ll never know because the song was hugely successful for a song of that time, it got over five-thousand recordings world-wide, you know that’s including all the foreign language recordings. It was a very successful song.
It sounds like the Louise Fletcher syndrome.

Yeah or the Rita Moreno syndrome when she won for, West Side Story. She had been getting all kinds of parts before that, then all of a sudden she got typed as a Puerto Rican. I didn’t get typed, I have no idea to this day why that happened. People used to say, “Gee, maybe they thought your price went up to high.” I said, “Nobody ever asked.”
[they both laugh]
So, did you do, The Russians are Coming, shortly after that?
I did, yes.
From which came another really great tune, “The Shining Sea.”
Um-hm, and before that I did a horrible picture called, An American Dream, from which came, “A Time for Love.”
Yeah, An American Dream, I’ve only seen the title listed with the song, I never saw the film or heard anything about it.
You haven’t missed a thing.
[laughs]

It was a dramatization of a Norman Mailer novel, and it was the most violent God­ damn picture I’ve ever seen. And I was busy writing – but it did have a nightclub scene it, your usual cliché and I was able to get that song in there, for which I’m glad. And everybody on the picture hated the song, they said, “It doesn’t fit the picture,” well of course it didn’t fit the picture, you couldn’t write a love song to fit that picture.
[they both laugh]
How about…

I mean, it’s about a man who kills his wife by pushing her off the roof of a twenty- five, thirty story building and gets away with it or tries to get away with it. You know it’s a totally repugnant, violent picture, the way it was shot, the dialogue itself which was Mailer dialogue, you know it was just not good Norman Mailer writing.
And so the film kind of went to well deserved oblivion.
Oh immediately, if there had been cable then, it would have gone straight to it, if they had allowed it on the air.
[laughs] How about, Harper?

Oh, Harper, I did after, The Russians are Coming. Russians are Coming was a very nice experience, that was with Norman Jewison, and Hal Ashby was the editor and Hal and I had been friends for many years before that so it was just a nice experience. Good actors, it was a good movie, very good movie for its day. Got to work with large choruses on that, where we had to sound – sort of ape the Red Army chorus for all the Russian parts of the picture. I had a huge chorus from UCLA and it was all the writing was in Russian.
Wow, so they had to learn all that phonetically?

Had to learn it all phonetically, yeah. We got a bunch of students and we made sure they were very scared because we wanted them to not come in – we didn’t use trained session singers, we used kids that we tried to psyche up to sing way beyond their capacity. Pretty much like soldiers who were having bayonets pointed at them, which I’m sure happened in Russia at that time. And that was the sound, you know they were singing for all they were worth, like their lives depended on it. I think we told them something stupid like if they didn’t do well, or didn’t know their part they couldn’t sing on the track and they wouldn’t get paid, or they couldn’t do it. And they had the fear of God drilled into them by the time they got up there ‘cause we wanted

them to sing with that extra energy that you could only get doing that way, by being slightly frightened. So they gave a very good approximation of a large military chorus, well a Red Army chorus, there is no other chorus like that in the world. There still isn’t.
[Interruption, D.A.T. recording switch to Tape 4]
Anyway, we were talking about, The Russians are Coming, and the Red Army chorus imitation and from that movie came, “The Shining Sea.”
Yeah.
That Peggy Lee did the lyric for right?

Right, that was done after the movie, we realized we had something that could be a song and Peggy Lee did an amazing thing, to me. She is a very intuitive lady, but I gave her this theme and I asked her, “Would you like to write a lyric to it?” And she said, “Yes,” and she wrote it and it was written for – and I saw the lyric and I said, “How did you do that,” she said, “how did I do what?” I said, “This song which I didn’t tell you about was actually written for a scene that takes place in a movie called, The Russians are Coming, The Russians are Coming, and you described in that lyric exactly what takes place on the screen at the time this music is playing,” I said, “how did you do that?” She says, “I don’t know.” And I said, “What are you doing tonight,” and I took her to a private screening of the thing, we were still in the rough form, you know, or we were just starting to preview it. And her mouth just fell open, she said, “Oh my God,” she said, “Well I don’t know, that spoke to me in that way and you must have captured whatever it was,” so I guess but you know she’s the kind of lady that would pick that up.
So…
So, that’s how that one came about.
It’s an underrated tune I think and it should be better known than it is.

Um-hm, it’s one of those songs that’s a little, not obscure but it’s… yeah, it’s not very well known, it’s one of those songs a little like, “You are There,” in the sense that the two songs aren’t similar but they tend to go in unproven paths. I just let that song write itself, I didn’t try to construct any particular kind of song and the same with, “You are There,” they just sort of came out that way and I let them go. Which I think is really the best way to write.
I think Bob Brookmeyer said that, “a lot of times I don’t have too much control over these things.”
It’s much better if I don’t.
[laughs]
‘Cause it’s the only way I can get out of my own way. “The Shadow,” came out all like that, I wrote it in about fifteen minutes, “Emily,” too.
Really?
Yeah, sure, wrote, “The Shadow,” in an all night restaurant back in the good ol’ days before they had music everywhere. When you could go into a place and get silence.
So you wrote it in a restaurant, does that mean that you do a lot of your song writing away from the piano?
Songwriting yes. I think that’s the best way to write your songs, I think a good song will hold up, a capella, a bad song will not. That’s one of the rules I have.
Yeah, now that I think of it, some of the songs I’ve written, I’ve written the melodies first and added the chords later.

Yeah, I mean I used to do what a lot of other people did, get a chord pattern and then fit the melody over it, that’s what’s wrong with most pop tunes of the day. It’s, you know, they’ll get a riff, they’ll get a chord pattern and they’ll just bebop over it you know and write – and then the melody to fit the chords and such, that is not songwriting.
Now-a-days you’re lucky if…
At least not by my kind of…
Now-a-days you’re lucky if the songs have chords.
You’re very lucky if they have chords, or if they have more than two or three. Most of them don’t, I just decided never to pay attention to that.
Now, so, after, The Russians are Coming, came, Harper, with Paul Newman, from which came, “Sure as You’re Born.”
Um-hm, which was never meant to be a song but somehow became because that was the era where they turned everything into a song, they just put a lyric to it.
Do you think that the success that Mancini had with some of the songs that came from his movies had something to do with that? Things like, “Moon River, “ and, “Charade,” and what have you?

No, that started a long time ago in 1952 with the title song when Dimitri Tiomkin wrote, “High Noon.” The title song was really with us all through the 50s and it wasn’t necessarily a good thing but it was a good thing for song writers.
I guess even earlier with, “Laura,” for example.
That was a freak ‘cause it started life as an instrumental theme, it wasn’t even sung in the movie.
That’s…
And Johnny Mercer wrote a lyric to it later on.

Well, some things, my memory is starting to fail me around then. I did… I’d have to go look at credits and things to remember.
But I guess the next major one would be, MASH.

Probably, MASH was 1970. I’ve done some pictures I’d rather not remember, like, Some Kind of a Nut, and I did, That Cold Day in the Park, for Bob Altman before MASH. Convoluted tale, we were – did you see the movie?
Yes.

So, that’s – what that is is a lesson, which is never throw anything away because you never know what’s gonna happen with a song. People had told me that before like…Jay Livingston and Ray Evans had a song in a C picture, it wasn’t even a B picture called, Captain Carey, U.S.A., which was probably one of the worst pictures ever made and the song was, “Mona Lisa,” for which they won the Academy Award and it became just this gigantic song. You just, you never throw anything away [laughs] so that’s what happened with MASH. And doing the music was a lot of fun, I had brought the Japanese jazz band, I’d heard some records about 1949, probably the first Japanese jazz records that ever came out and they were so horrible and they were so funny because they were so horrible I just fell on the floor laughing

and somehow I remembered that. And when I started seeing – you remember those things we did like the Pidgin, “My Blue Heaven,” and things like that. Well the early Japanese jazz records were just dreadful, they played them instead of [sings standard boogie-woogie] boogie-woogie was in 6/8 [sings boogie-woogie in 6/8]
[they both laugh]
And they became wonderful jazz musicians later on but they hadn’t caught on yet in 1949.

The next one I know…
A lot of fun.
Sounds like it.

Uh-huh.

Let’s see, I did before that I probably did, Summer Wishes, Winter Dreams, which was Death of a Snow Queen in its original form with Joanne Woodward. Got a nice little song out of that, they wrote with Alan and Marilyn Bergman called, “Summer Wishes, Winter Dreams,” fittingly enough. In fact they liked the – they changed the title of the movie to that. And then, God, you know I really forget what I do. Did Agatha, had fun with that, got a song out of it, “Close Enough for Love.” Wonderful director on that, Michael Apted, great director, this man could photograph the longest master shots I ever saw. And I did a lot of good pictures during that time, not too long after that I did Deathtrap with Sidney Lumet. And I did some Rock n’ Roll movies, I did, Staying Alive.
Oh, you did that one?

Yeah, I did. Which was really, Saturday Night Fever, part two. And what else did I do, I don’t know, I did a string of movies, I did another one with Sidney Lumet which was a nice challenge which was – actually Deathtrap was quite a challenge, the whole thing was written mostly in the style of Bach and I used two harpsichords with Ralph Grierson and Mike Lang on them. Wrote a lot of Baroque music for that and I’d do things, talk about strange registers for instruments, I did, I would write, I wrote for some big pipe organs, I wrote like the two foot stops, four foot stops on the harpsichord in the very low register, as low as I could get them and the sixteen foot stops in the very high register, you know I’d do it just the – I did that just the, you know would do things like that to get unusual timbres. And it was a very interesting thing to do, plus you know did the harpsichords – had a large orchestra too. Oh, let’s see what else we
did, did, The Verdict with Sidney Lumet in the 80s, that was with a large chorus and orchestra. Very nice lovely film to do.
How did you learn to write for voices? We didn’t talk about that at all.
I never did, I just started doing it. I’d look at – I’d listen to what other people did with voices and figure that out and just started writing myself.
Any vocal writing that in particular influenced you that you can think of?

No. No. I don’t have a very strong vocal style. I just write chorally like Mancini did and in the case of, The Verdict say, or… I went with the genre whichever you do, I was there I was writing almost Gregorian chants in a lot of cases. And in the case of like, The Russians are Coming, I was writing very modal and very Russian type of music. You know you go with what – there’s a reason for using voices to start with, you’re generally either dealing with a nationality or a period because I don’t believe in using voices in movies I think they’re death because there’s nothing that will eat up dialogue faster and pull your ear away from dialogue.
It’s competitive.
Very, there’s nothing as stirring or powerful in pulling your ear as the human voice. People just start listening to it, whether they want to or not. So…
Well, so then why are rock ‘n’ roll soundtracks so popular with movies now?

Well, it’s certainly terrible cinematic and also I’m discovering that more and more that the kids that are making movies now for the most part don’t know what they’re doing, there’s no taste there and they’re interested in – I’m trying not to sound like an old fogey, but the emphasis is more on the soundtrack album really than it is on helping the picture a great deal. Occasionally you get movies where it works nicely like, Sleepless in Seattle, it’s nice to see a main title and see like – hear Jimmy Durante doing, “As Time Goes By,” you know it’s, there’s something very touching about it. The rock, most rock – you’re finding, I’m finding less and less rock tracks now, they’re going more towards older timey music and the thing like I did with Kevin Kline just recently on, French Kiss.
Where you arranged, “La Mer.”

“La Mer,” yeah, the old Charles Trenet tune, which was also the thing Bobby Darin made a hit on as “Beyond the Sea,” back in the 50s. We didn’t do it that way though, we did it more a traditional way.
Do you get the impression that say the pendulum is swinging back a bit from say the mid-80s where…
Everything was synthesized, yes.
The, Miami Vice trend.

Yeah, back to… live orchestras and things like that, I find more and more of that yeah and I’m very happy to see it. The only problem is during the 60s, 70s and 80s they tore down all the large studios that we used to record that stuff in and it’s hard to find good big rooms. There’s only one in New York that I know of and that’s the Hit Factory. And also you have run into trouble, you know we’re doing a lot of, I’ve been doing nothing but large orchestra things for the last five years for people, you know whether it’s in movies, or whether it’s in making records with Natalie Cole or with Shirley Horn or Tony Bennett or anybody. And there’s only so many large rooms in town now, they need to build some more now that they’re starting to hire musicians and put synthesizer players out of work.
Well Sony has built a new studio, right? With a…
Here? Yes.
That can accommodate a large orchestra?
Yeah, but I don’t think they – I think they keep it for Sony artists, I don’t know if they let anyone else in there, do they?
I don’t know. I think you’re right.
It would be wonderful if they did because we need rooms in this town and I hate to see one room getting all the business.
I hear there’s one in Astoria.

Yeah but that’s a long way to go. A long way to go. Its one thing if you’re shooting there and you know need all the facilities to shoot, you need a sound stage, the things you can’t get in Manhattan but you’re not going to truck a whole bunch of musicians out there just to

record. You know its one thing to do a jazz date out with Rudy Van Gelder, but getting a huge orchestra into Astoria, yeah, you can do it I suppose. I don’t know what their recording facilities are like out there either, whether they’re prehistoric from the old days ‘cause you know the original film studios were out in those parts of New York before they moved to California.
With the scarcity of record and film dates now, I think if you told somebody that you had a date for them in Astoria, they’d be there.

Well you know something as I was just saying what I said about travelling that distance, it’s not really that far when you think of the distances we travel in California for God- sakes, just going from Burbank to Culver City is further than going from Manhattan to Astoria. Absolutely, and takes longer…
Yeah.
Especially with the freeways the way they are. [laughs]
So, you told me recently that you basically weren’t interested in writing, quote “backgrounds for films anymore.”
I am not, at all, I’ve done it.
When did you make that decision?

I’ve been working towards that decision all through the 80s, even – I started getting very disenchanted with it in the 70s, I keep thinking of movies I did during that, as I talk about it, that I remember around the time I was doing, Freaky Friday, and, Escape to Witch Mountain out at Disney I was staring to really want to do records more and films, I’d have loved to have gotten rid of films. I don’t like writing background, that much and developing – I’ve never wanted to personally write large works, symphonies, concert pieces or I’d have done it. ‘Cause developing material is, I can do it, I’ve certainly had to do it enough for movies, but it’s not really what I get the most satisfaction out of.
Because it struck me that you’d be a natural to do say what Mancini did and go out and do orchestra pops concerts and do your medley of hits.
Yes, I probably will.
I hope so.
Um-hm. I probably will.
Because I mean, you’ve probably got as many great tunes that people are aware of as Hank did, if you were to go down the list of them.

Well, it’s growing and I’m happy to hear you say that. Hank Mancini is – left very big shoes to fill though, I’ll tell you that. He was my ideal of what the perfect composer was for films for pops, for almost anything. He was so elegant in everything he did; he did it right and on top of it he was a marvelous human being.
He did everything he did with a lot of class.
Oh he had class, indeed he did.
And I guess his success with, Peter Gunn and Mr. Lucky, really opened the door for a lot of writers in Hollywood.
It sure did. It sure did. For a while there they were trying to put jazz scores to everything and it was quite laughable.
Yeah.

Because jazz scores fit a very tiny fraction of the movies that people tried to put – rock ‘n’ roll really fits a very tiny fraction too. More of the pictures now are conducive to rock ‘n’ roll, you see a piece of film like, Pulp Fiction, and I couldn’t envision using anything but rock ‘n’ roll in that thing.
Well as you got into the 80s and you decided to put film more in the background and recording more in the foreground…
Um-hm.
Well some of the projects, we’ve talked about the Shirley Horn project, we’ve only talked peripherally about the Natalie Cole, Unforgettable, [Unforgettable… with Love] album.
Yeah, that was a very nice project to do.
That you got a Grammy for right?
Correct, yeah I did.
For the arrangement for, “Unforgettable,” or…
Um-hm.
How – you did several of the charts right?
I did about nine of them, yeah.
And I think Bill Holman and Alan Broadbent also did some.
Yeah they did some, I probably did the majority of the album.
Do you want to talk about your experience with Natalie?
Yeah, she’s delightful to work with. She’s a total professional, comes in, knows everything, just sings like an angel. What more can you ask? She’s very talented.
And a nice person to deal with I’m told.
Yeah. Yeah, Natalie’s fine.
Now the concept of her singing along with her father’s vocal tracks, who came up with that?

She started doing it – I don’t know who originally had the idea, she started doing it in nightclubs as part of her act. A year or two before she – you know in her show she used to do a Nat Cole segment and then she found that she had this – she did have from his TV show a recording of, “Unforgettable,” on film and she started flashing it on the screen. Somebody came up with that idea, maybe she came up with it, I don’t know, she might have practiced it on TV first with a videocassette. And she discovered she could do this to, “Unforgettable,” and you could only do that because it was a song on which it sat on one chord for two bars, so you could get all those answers in. You couldn’t do that with other songs, that’s why that’s the only song it got done on.
There are more holes to be filled there.

Well the holes, you could – it was a natural for answers because you had the same chord, you weren’t switching chords, you’d have F [sings F] A-flat diminished two bars, G- minor seven two bars [sings G-minor] B-flat minor six two bars, et cetera, et cetera, the whole song went like that. So, you’re limited on the songs you could do that with. But it worked on

this one and it seemed to get a great deal of attention in the room when she did it in clubs, so I guess the natural thing to think about was when she decided she wanted to make an album of her father’s stuff she – Natalie had heard the Linda Ronstadt, got Nelson Riddle and all that and then Nelson died so she couldn’t get Nelson again like her father had so I got the call. And that’s what we did.
Do you think that that particular CD had a great deal of influence on other people doing projects, say you know middle of the road pop vocal projects with large orchestras?

Oh it must have yeah, I think everybody started trying to do 40s albums there for a while with the – but it was great because a lot – I think all these things like Linda Ronstadt, you know people were critical about at the time, they like to snipe at other people, particularly those who’ve been successful like, she didn’t know how to sing the songs and all that sort of thing well nobody would tell you that quicker than Linda. She had to learn how to sing that kind of music, where Natalie didn’t ‘cause it was the most natural thing in the world for her. But for the first time they started, for the first time a lot of people had never heard the sound of a full orchestra like that. Particularly the kids and they liked it, they went out and bought that. You know they’d heard the full orchestra in the movies but they’d never heard it on records, unless they dug out old records. And most of that was their parent’s music. So, yeah, it started putting musicians to work more and they started using it for end titles in movies, it wasn’t just all synthesizers. And, worked out to be a good thing and we put a lot of synthesizer players out of work, at least two of them. Who are each busy putting fifty musicians out of work.
Wasn’t that Conte Candoli’s line?
Oh, I think it’s been used a lot of times.
[laughs] You did something – some of the credits you’ve been listed with lately have included what, well, the Manhattan Transfer Christmas album.
Oh yeah, that was fun. I loved doing that.
For which you have…
They’re a great group to work for, with.
For which you have a Christmas tune on there.
That’s true, yeah.
“All I Want for Christmas is You.”
Well, that isn’t the name of it, it’s called, “The Christmas Song.”
Uh-huh.
“A Christmas Love Song,” excuse me, “The Christmas Song,” is, “Chestnuts,” the Mel Tormé song.
Did you write it specifically for that recording?
No, no, I just wrote the song and it came out sounding like Christmas, I didn’t try to write a Christmas song.
Um-hm.

I said for some reason this sounds like Christmas, I don’t know what makes a song sound like Christmas, I probably wrote it in July or something and took it to the Bergman’s and they said, “Yeah, that sounds like a Christmas song.” And then Marilyn said, “What makes it sound like a Christmas song?” And I says, “I really don’t know and I’m afraid if I try to figure it out how I did it I probably couldn’t do it again.”
So you did that, you did part of an album with Diane Schuur, some of those arrangements.
Yeah, I just done a bunch of stuff.
Michael Feinstein.
Did produce that, I’ve produced all these albums you’re speaking of too.
Right, so your producing career kind of blossomed in the 80s right?
Yes, it did. I’ve wanted to produce records for twenty years and it’s very hard to get producing work, for somebody like me.
How did you make it happen?
What, how did it happen?
What buttons did you push, who did you talk to, who opened some doors for you?
I had to wait until they wanted the arrangements badly enough.
[laughs]
If you want to know the truth and I just said, “Well, you gotta take the whole package.”
It’s nice that you had that kind of leverage.

Well when it happened I definitely took advantage of it and I really like, I love producing records and particularly ‘cause I just like to run my own store, I like to conceive the song jointly with the artist, or by myself and take it right up through the mastering to the time the thing hits the street and leaves the studio. I like to do the whole thing and it’s frustrating to me when I deliver it to someone else and they take it and do what they want with it. That’s the kind of feeling you often got in movies, too. I hear the finished product and I want to get it as close to the finished product that I heard as possible in my head, initially. That’s why producing is really part of it.
That’s one of the reasons Marion Evans got out of the music business isn’t it, because he got so bugged with things being out of his control that he was – mixes that he was unhappy with?
Probably, I just never discussed that with him, but I imagine that would’ve been one of the reasons. It’s you know, it’s something that happens to everyone and I can’t say that I enjoyed it one bit.
What did you do with Michael Jackson?

Oh, I wrote quite a bit for Michael over the years. With and without Quincy Jones, he didn’t write I mean but… when Quincy was producing Michael I worked on the Off the Wall album, I worked with him on – I can’t remember whether I worked on Thriller or not. I worked on Dangerous, which he did by himself. Michael’s wonderful to work with, he’s the most professional man I’ve ever seen in the studio.
No kidding.
Yeah.
Why is that? What…

He just knows everything that’s happening and never gets in your way and doesn’t get in his. He’s ideal, when he’s in the studio he has absolutely no ego, he’s considerate of everyone, he’s great, everybody loves to work with him.
What do you do on those projects? What…
Usually, the big string arrangements, or any time he wants kind of a lush sound for anything. I don’t do all the synthesizer stuff.
It’s interesting he…
‘Cause there’s plenty of guys who do that better than I do, although I use synthesizers all the time, myself, I like them as part of the orchestra.
I’ve noticed on the dates of yours that I’ve been attending at that you’ll always have a DX7 [Yamaha Digital Synthesizer] there, even with a large string orchestra.
I sure will.
What do you use the DX for?

A number of things, I’ll use it for – well it makes the best [inaudible] sounds for one thing. I’ll usually have a full setup though not just the DX, I’ll have the full complement of synthesizers. I’ll use it sometimes when I’m writing a lot of, like big orchestra and I want to take all my strings up in the air, like I want the violins to play something, the viocellos maybe to play a counter line and so I’ve lost all my strings to play the sustaining type of harmonic support and a lot of times rather than use all the wind instruments for that ‘cause I want them to do something else I’ll very often, I’ll do some magic and use – split my instruments up so I have some of it covered down there but I’ll use the synthesizers for reinforcement but in a way that you never hear them, you just feel them. I make sure you never hear them because I don’t want it to sound like synthesizers at any time.
With a smaller string section would you use a synth just to bolster the string sound?
If I had to but I don’t like it and I’ll usually turn down projects like that if I can help it. Or limit the string writing into registers where they won’t sound too terrible with a small section.
It’s interesting, Michael Jackson has used you quite a bit for things of that nature, Prince uses Clare Fischer.
Um-hm.
That’s very little noted, that they use orchestrators of your and his caliber for their projects. I think…
Jeremy Lubbock does tons of that stuff.
Yeah.
And I’ve worked a lot with David Foster doing all those kinds of records.

So let’s see, we’ve touched on a lot of stuff, what I’d like to do in the remaining time is just talk about, I’ve got a list of ever tune of yours that I could think of or you know conjure up in reference books, I’d just like to run them by you and get any comments that you’d like to make on any of them. Some…
Okay.
[Slight pause]
Johnny, I’m just gonna run a list of your tunes by you in no particular order and some of them we’ve already discussed but any comments that come to mind fire away. “Just a Child.”
“Just a Child,” I had a tune to write – that I wanted to write for a Bill Perkins album and I’d wanted to write a song of that kind and that's what I wrote at that time.
That's one of your earliest songs really isn’t it?

Yeah. I still thought of it in instrumental terms I never tried to get a lyric to it. I didn’t even try to get a lyric to any of the, I Want to Live! songs but I guess I always really wrote songs kind of like Al Cohn did and like – what we wrote were really songs. Tiny Kahn, Neal Hefti, we wrote melodically, it was just that simple, so I guess, oh being born in the 1920s we were structured, however unconsciously to think of themes as songs because we didn’t come for classical backgrounds and the popular music of the day made a big imprint on us. The thirty-two bar song, blues, and that sort of thing. So, I’d write an instrumental and it would tend – I would try to make it melodic just because I wanted to have some kind of an identifiable melody, but I didn’t know, I never thought about whether I was good at it or not ‘cause I was never interested in writing songs. To me the worst, the worst kind of existence was being like the guys I used to see around the Brill building [New York City] scurrying around with songs under their arms, I
was so grateful I could arrange I just didn’t want to do that. It seemed like, I probably couldn't – the idea of all that rejection did not appeal to me.
“Quietly There.”
It’s just a song that I wrote…
For, Harper, right?
Yeah, yeah. I didn’t really write it for, Harper, it’s just something that I came up with and I put it into, Harper, as a piece of source music but it wasn't really written for that movie.
The lyric is by Morgan Ames right?
Came later, yeah.
Is that the only song that you wrote with her?
No, no. We wrote, “Unless It’s You,” and we just now wrote something, just finished a song called, “Life in My Eyes,” brand new song.
“Emily.”
“Emily,” was written for…
The Americanization…
The Americanization of Emily.
With Johnny Mercer right?

Right, it started with a motif that I thought fitted the character that Julie Andrews played. You know [sings Emily, Emily] I wanted to get kind of a sort of a purity in a nice ethereal way, type of feeling, it seemed to capsulize what she was to me at that time. And the song just kind of spun itself out one night.
Gene Lees tells a nice story about, The Singers Unlimited, recording of that tune.
Um-hm.
Do you want to tell it?
I don't know it.

He wrote in a liner note to one of The Singers Unlimited albums that one day he wanted to know a couple of chords in “Emily,” so he picked up the phone and called you and you told him what it was and he wrote it down and you said, “You got that? Now throw those away and go to, The Singers Unlimited recording and use those changes.”
Did I say that?
That’s what Gene said.

Well, then I’m sure I did ‘cause I adore the way Gene Puerling writes. I was fortunate enough to work with him again on the – well not again but I mean work with him for the first time really on the Manhattan Transfer album we both wrote choral arrangements for that. In fact we split tunes, I’d write part of it, he’d write part, that sort of thing.
“Groover Wailin’.”

Just trying to put – just wrote it for instrumental. It was a play upon the guy who used to in the 30s, for some reason don't ask me why, I had some strange titles in my time, this guy was Grover Whalen and he was the official receptionist for New York. He used to lead all the tickertape parades for all the heroes that came in and he was sort of like the, he was the big guy all through the 20s, 30s and even 40s. He was a well known name and people around who heard that title would have known who I was talking about, nobody would know it now. And it was written for the Cy Touff, Richie Kamuca album, I just needed some kind of a fast instrumental and that’s what I wrote.
And Bill Perkins recorded it later.
May have, yeah.
“El Cajon.”

I wrote something for Al Cohn and decided to title it that. El Cajon is the name of a pass outside of Los Angeles, what’s it mean El Cajon? The… cajon… I don’t know, it means something in Spanish but El Cajon Pass I always thought sounded like Al Cohn so when the time came to use it, I used it. And then Dave Frishberg wrote a very amusing lyric keeping the title.
[laughs] We talked about, “A Time For Love,” and, “The Shadow of Your Smile,” anything to add to those two?
No, I think I’ve said it all.
“Sure as You’re Born.”

“Sure as You're Born,” came to be called, “Sure as You're Born,” it was originally the main title theme from, Harper and it didn't stay that way very long because before the picture was released Alan Bergman came up with a lyric. The Warner Brothers called them and had – I’d never met them before, I’d met them but never worked with them and all of a sudden there they were in the studio one day at an appointment with the lyric. And like everything they write it was – she never, they never wrote a word that didn't sing. They are one of the most professional lyric writers I’ve ever run into with the exception of Johnny Mercer.
They did, “Quietly There,” as well, right?
No, Morgan Ames.
Oh that’s right, Morgan did. They did, “Where Do You Start.”
Yeah, we’re still writing, we’re writing all the time. We've got a brand-new one we just finished, which I would play you if I had a piano.
I’d love to hear it.
Um-hm.
“Keester Parade.”
That was a play on Easter Parade, keester was a very popular term amongst musicians in the 40s – 30s, 40s and 50s for a girls derrière.
It’s just as a simple blues basically.
It basically is yeah.
“The Shining Sea,” we talked about.
Yes.
“Something Different.”
The stupidest song I could ever think of, that should never have been recorded by anyone.
[laughs]

It was written to see how far you can stretch a stupid little motif, it was, if you could hear it the way I originally played it on the piano, you’d laugh. Bill Perkins actually made a record of it and I was totally aghast when he did it.
[laughs] Theme from MASH we talked about. “Where Do You Start?”

“Where Do You Start?” had a very interesting, that had a very interesting genealogy. A well-known playwright, who will remain unnamed, liked to write lyrics and one of them came my way and strangely enough this is another one of those things like the Peggy Lee story. He wrote a lyric about a breakup of his marriage or relationship, I guess it was autobiographical, I don’t know. But I was asked, you know the lyric came my way and I wrote the music to it and then after I finished it, I said, “Gee this sounds like a pretty decent saloon song, but this is not much of a lyric, the man should stick to playwriting.” But what caught my interest, was that it had a very different rhyme scheme, you know it was arrhythmic or asymmetrical… it caught my eye as a thing to write to. So I brought it to Alan and Marilyn Bergman ‘cause I wanted a lyric and they took the song and came up with the identical subject material that I had evidently caught from the first lyric.
Wow.

So whether I evoked it in the music or not I'll never know ‘cause I never told them a thing about it. Then after they finished it, I mean right away when they brought it to me I said, “Oh, boy, this is the definitive divorce song,” and then I showed them the original lyric and they did the same kind of like, the eyes bugged out and mouth feel open, you know they said, “Wow.”
[laughs]
Wow. “You Are There.”

“You Are There,” is just one of those songs that emerged one morning, I was on my way to an appointment and I stopped the car and wrote it down, it all came out in one – it’s the kind of a song that you’d never set out to write and I didn’t know what to do with that song, I had five different lyrics to it before Dave Frishberg came up with the – and he wrote the last two of them. I got… three of them before and they just didn't make it, they didn’t even come close.

Frishberg took it, he wrote a lyric and he said, “Nah, I can do better than that,” so he wrote and then next one he wrote was, “You Are There.” And Dave Frishberg is one of the best lyricists I’ve ever written with, he can do anything. He’s as close to Johnny Mercer as you can get.
High praise.
Indeed.
“I Wish I’d Met You.”

I wrote that totally to a lyric, Richard Rodney Bennett sent me a lyric he had written, you know Richard Rodney Bennett’s a rather famous composer in his own right and a wonderful film composer. He had written, you know, Equus, also for Sidney Lumet, Far From the Madding Crowd…
Enchanted April.

Enchanted April, he writes wonderful scores, even Four Weddings and a Funeral, I think. He didn’t get much to do in that, but you know he writes wonderful movie scores, ballets, hell of a good piano player, does a good cabaret act. Likes to sing and write songs, I never knew that about him…
[Interruption: Phone rings]
You were talking about Richard Rodney Bennett and his various skills and we were going to talk about the lyric he wrote for…

Oh, yeah, he, Richard and a lyric writer he likes to write with sometimes Frank Underwood, who lives down in the village here. They sent me the song and they said we’d like to get a melody for this and I’d written some “Lovers After All,” previously with Richard and he heard the song and said, “Can I do that?” And I said, “Sure, go ahead.” And so he sent me this and he said, “We don’t have a song and also we don’t have a title,” and I said, “Yeah, you have a title, “I Wish I’d Met You,” [laughs] it was right there. And I just wrote the song from the lyric, I like working that way as I’ve told you.
Yes.

‘Cause it makes me go places I wouldn't normally go. Even, The Sandpiper, the first shot of writing lyrics, I mean writing to lyrics, I wrote the verse to Paul Webster's lyric. You know I wrote the melody first and then he said, “you know something, It’d be nice to have a

verse for this song, explaining something, tying it into the picture better,” so he wrote the verse and I wrote the melody right over the phone with him. I phoned him back in about five minutes with it, it just worked out that way, I found that it was not a hard thing to do. And that's what I did with, “I Wish I’d Met You,” just wrote – and I wrote it to MASH too and a lot of other songs I wrote to lyric. The one we just talked about, “Where Do You Start,” to a lyric.
“Cinnamon and Clove.”

“Cinnamon and Clove,” I’d just come back from Brazil and wanted to write in that idiom and that's what I wrote. And gave it to Alan and Marilyn and they just came up with, “Cinnamon and Clove,” which actually came from a Jorge Amado novel, a Brazilian, really great Brazilian novelist – a Brazilian writer, he wrote all kinds of things called… Gabriela, Cloves and Cinnamon [Gabriela, Cravo e Canela] which later on was made into a movie for which Jobim [Antonio Carlos Brasileiro de Almeida Jobim] wrote the music, you know, many years later.
“I Never Told You.”

That was written, not to be a song, it was written as a theme for, That Cold Day in the Park, which was the first movie I wrote with Robert Altman, I mean that I did with Robert Altman, the picture with Sandy Dennis. And I said, “Well gee, maybe there’s a song there,” ‘cause that was the theme I used in the main title, as an instrumental with Bud Shank playing the flute and it was really nice, it seemed – it came out nicely so I sent it to Arthur Hamilton and it became, “I Never Told You.”
Toots Thielemans did a wonderful recording of it with Quincy.
Oh yeah, with Quincy Jones.
Yeah. Let’s see, that's all the songs I came up with, what did I miss?

Oh God, I don’t know, there’s the one Lena Horne recorded recently, “I’ll Always Leave the Door a Little Open,” in her most recent album. That happened exactly like, “I Wish I'd Met You,” Richard Rodney Bennett and Frank Underwood sent me the lyric they said, “We need a song, Lena wants to do this lyric,” I said, “great,” and I sent him the song.
[Interruption]
[laughs]
Alright it's really been a fucking drag these last eight hours, I don't know why we did this…
[laughs loudly]
And I hope you'll burn it.
[they both laugh]
As a friend of mine once said, “Don’t say fuck in front of the K.I.D.S.”
Oh, okay.
[they both laugh]
It wasn’t too long that I saw a woman when I was in New York, on a snowy day, step into the gutter and yell, “Oh shit, I just stepped in dog poo poo!”
[they both laugh]
You know the only thing I wanted to ask you, you’ve had the tribute of having a number of musicians and singers record all Johnny Mandel records. Sue Raney did one.
Yeah.
Bill Perkins did one.
Yeah.
Fred Hersch has a new one out.
I know he does, does a wonderful job on…
I haven't heard it yet. I’ll bet he does.

He takes songs to a different place than anyone else would. It's very transparent and he picks different tempos than any else – you know that I would ever think of and it's wonderful to hear somebody take things and do something you wouldn't think of with them.
Who else has done records like that?
Actually not that many people, there are very few… albums of all my stuff, very few. Hopefully maybe someday they'll be more.
I would hope so.

Tony Bennett said he like to do one of all my stuff. He's done an awful lot of it as it is. He made the definitive records on, on “Emily,” on, “A Time For Love,” on, “The Shadow of Your Smile.” Did a real nice one on, “The Shining Sea,” that's already a third of an album. He wants to do, “Unless It’s You,” he wants to do, “Where Do You Start?” I just wrote a brand new song for him with Alan and Marilyn that he won't do because the lyrics remind him too much of his ex-wife.
[they both laugh]
You never know what you run into with singers.
It’s highly subjective.

Got a couple of more, several lyrics that he would like – several songs he’d like very much like, “I Won’t Believe My Eyes,” which you've never heard. There’s a lot of songs I’ve got you haven't heard. And it's on-going, I’ve got several songs that I haven’t uncorked at all yet.
You have one book published of…
Yeah, oh, that's actually in that book, “I Won’t Believe My Eyes.”
Are you going to do any further books like that?
Sure, if somebody asks me.
Who published the one that's out?
Hal Leonard published that out.
That’s right.

And they’re going to put it out again without the cassette, they found that hampered sales a great deal because you know the cassette is sitting right up in the front of the book and I did that on purpose because I wanted it to be partly a tutorial so that people could get their hands on the music more because nobody reads music now like they did back in the 20s and 30s and

40s when everybody had a piano in the house and that was the cheap form of entertainment. Somebody in the family could always, usually, not often but more often than now could fumble around and had had some piano lessons and could pick out the popular song of the day in however rudimentary a fashion. Now people can’t even read a fake book which, I think I might've said that yesterday somewhere along the line, which is just the bare chords and melody, like the most, you know basic way of conveying a song. They can't read that, there's even a book out on how to read a fake book. That is true.
In our…

So, that's why I put the cassette in the book but the dealers hate to – you can’t display it properly with the cassette, they can't what they call, “rack them.” So, they’re gonna put it out now without the cassette after several years, they figure the sales will do much better but I've written more song since then so I’d like to probably do an updated version sooner or later.
That would be great.
Probably with Warner's, I’ll go to them.
I guess the only thing I haven’t asked you, is about who your favorite songwriters are and film composers are.
Okay, well how many hours have we got left?
[they both laugh]

Favorite songwriters, my God, you know the old phrase, “We stand on the shoulders of giants,” there are so many giants and I’m fortunate enough to be on the board of governors of ASCAP, I have been for the past six years and you run into these giants, or their ghosts up their because it was founded, one of the founders was Irving Berlin who was really American music basically and has been for the last you know forty, fifty years. Oh God, Berlin, Jerome Kern, Richard Rodgers and Lorenz Hart, I preferred the early Rodgers by far to the later Rodgers. I mean we had so many wonderful writers, Harry Warren, Johnny Mercer, Vincent Youmans, you know with everyone I name there’s probably gonna be that many I forget. Fats Waller, Duke Ellington, you can just go on and on, Cole Porter, George Gershwin I haven’t even mentioned. There’s just – you know, what a tradition we have in back of us of songwriting and I’m sure I’ve forgotten a number of giants just right now and they’re wonderful. Did I say Vincent Youmans? You know you can just go on and on.
How about film writers?

Alex North, Alfred Newman, Max Steiner was a real hero, Victor Young was wonderful, Hugo Friedhofer, David Raksin wrote wonderfully. The ones that are around now, Johnny Williams wonderful all around writer. Jerry Goldsmith, Hank Mancini for sure, Dave Grusin great, you know there’s some good writers out there and again we are standing on the shoulders of giants. Bronislaw Kaper, I love and also a great songwriter. Wrote, Invitation and Green Dolphin Street, “All God’s Chillun Got Rhythm.” Broni who had quite a great sense of humor, I’ve heard, once on a talk show… the host was asking him, “You write these great symphonic scores and then you turn around and write a song like, “All God’s Chillun Got Rhythm,” how can this all come out of the same man?” And Broni said, “It’s very simple, I’m a phony.”
[They both laugh]
So, I’ll close with that I think.
[they both laugh]
So…

Cy Coleman, who’s on the board with me, there’s a real writer. Burton Lane who’s on the board with me, you talk about legends, you don’t – it doesn’t get any better than that. Jule Styne, you just left us, you know, you just go on and on. One great one after another.
Yeah, lets…

Boy, it’s wonderful just to be among all that and to be able to – we have such great literature to – you know this is the great treasury of American art, is the songwriting that has come out of this century of American music. And I’m just very proud to even however remotely, be associated with it.
Well, it’s far more than remotely as any number of people I think would attest.

Well, it’s an honor I’ll tell you that. And most of all to be able to have spent your life doing something you love, what more can you ask for? You know, that’s the most anybody can ask for and I was lucky enough to have it, and it ain’t over yet. Not by a long shot.
Unless you have something to add I couldn’t come up with a better ending line than
I think that wraps it up. Thank you very much.
Thank you Johnny.

segments.chapter: Childhood, schooling and the New York band scene
segments.title: Opening of the interview and birth in New York
segments.summary: Kirchner opens the tape and confirms Mandel's birth on November 23, 1925 on West End Avenue; he lived on the upper west side for his first seven years.

segments.chapter: Childhood, schooling and the New York band scene
segments.title: Parents, father's business and the move to California
segments.summary: Mandel names his parents and describes his father's cloak-and-suit business, which the Depression and the NRA ended; the family went to Los Angeles in 1934 and he mentions his sister Audrey.

segments.chapter: Childhood, schooling and the New York band scene
segments.title: A musical household and Uncle George
segments.summary: His mother was a frustrated opera singer; the house was full of jazz on radio and records, and his composer uncle George knew the Austin High gang and had Fats Waller visit.

segments.chapter: Childhood, schooling and the New York band scene
segments.title: Discovering the arranger through radio bands
segments.summary: Mandel started trumpet and arranging at twelve to thirteen, and explains how hearing different bands play the same song taught him that an arranger shapes the sound.

segments.chapter: Childhood, schooling and the New York band scene
segments.title: Back in New York in 1938 and the Robins family
segments.summary: Returning to New York at twelve, he hangs out with Marshall Robins and his publisher father Jack Robins, who takes the boys to hear bands in person until 4 a.m.

segments.chapter: Childhood, schooling and the New York band scene
segments.title: Early favorite bands and learning by ear
segments.summary: Mandel names the bands that impressed him as a listener, such as Goodman, Dorsey and Glenn Miller with Bill Finegan's writing, and says he learned to write by copying what he heard with perfect pitch.

segments.chapter: Childhood, schooling and the New York band scene
segments.title: Van Alexander's first lesson
segments.summary: Van Alexander shows him a score and plays the record, teaching him to associate written notes with sound, and then tells him to go home and write.

segments.chapter: Childhood, schooling and the New York band scene
segments.title: Writing in concert versus transposed scores
segments.summary: Mandel explains how he moved from transposed scores to writing in concert, mainly for speed on television and movie work.

segments.chapter: Childhood, schooling and the New York band scene
segments.title: Picking up instruments and not knowing strings
segments.summary: He learned the mechanics of instruments by fooling around with them, but knows nothing about playing strings and writes for them by ear.

segments.chapter: Childhood, schooling and the New York band scene
segments.title: Schools: PS 9, Tarrytown and New York Military Academy
segments.summary: Mandel recounts his schooling from PS 9 and Los Angeles public schools to a miserable boarding school at Tarrytown and then the Military Academy on a band scholarship, where he wrote for a dance band.

segments.chapter: Childhood, schooling and the New York band scene
segments.title: Hearing Charlie Barnet's band
segments.summary: Asked about bands heard live with Jack Robins, Mandel recalls loving Charlie Barnet's loose swinging band, its players and its arrangers.

segments.chapter: Childhood, schooling and the New York band scene
segments.title: Hotel rooms, theaters and the corny bands
segments.summary: He describes hearing bands at the Park Central, the New Yorker, the Astor and the stage shows, including Sammy Kaye and Guy Lombardo.

segments.chapter: Venuti, Billie Rogers and Henry Jerome
segments.title: Straight onto the road with Venuti and the wartime generation
segments.summary: Right out of high school Mandel joins Joe Venuti because musicians are scarce in wartime, and talks about Al Cohn, Getz and Zoot Sims coming up young into bands.

segments.chapter: Venuti, Billie Rogers and Henry Jerome
segments.title: Who was in Venuti's band
segments.summary: Mandel recalls Kay Starr, guitarist Hayden Causey, young Jimmy Raney and drummer Barrett Deems in Venuti's band.

segments.chapter: Venuti, Billie Rogers and Henry Jerome
segments.title: Venuti's practical joke on Paul Whiteman
segments.summary: Mandel tells a favorite Venuti story from 1930 in St. Louis, in which Joe hires two prostitutes to pose as his wife and mother at dinner with Whiteman.

segments.chapter: Venuti, Billie Rogers and Henry Jerome
segments.title: Working for Venuti and writing for him
segments.summary: Venuti disliked running a big band; Mandel stayed six to nine months and wrote backgrounds between one-nighters.

segments.chapter: Venuti, Billie Rogers and Henry Jerome
segments.title: The songbook piano tape
segments.summary: Mandel says he never learned piano, and explains that Mike Lang played the tape accompanying his songbook, voiced to sound good on piano.

segments.chapter: Venuti, Billie Rogers and Henry Jerome
segments.title: Billie Rogers's orchestra
segments.summary: After finishing school courses Mandel joined trumpeter-singer Billie Rogers's band until Christmas 1944 and praises her playing and singing.

segments.chapter: Venuti, Billie Rogers and Henry Jerome
segments.title: Switching to trombone and joining Henry Jerome
segments.summary: Realizing he would never be a good trumpeter, Mandel switched to slide trombone and rejoined Henry Jerome as first trombone.

segments.chapter: Venuti, Billie Rogers and Henry Jerome
segments.title: Henry Jerome band personnel
segments.summary: He names the musicians in Jerome's band, including Jack Eagle, Al Cohn, Lenny Garment and David Allyn, many of whom moved to Boyd Raeburn in June 1945.

segments.chapter: Venuti, Billie Rogers and Henry Jerome
segments.title: Alan Greenspan and Lenny Garment in the band
segments.summary: Mandel jokes that saxophonist Alan Greenspan did the payroll, and chats with Kirchner about Lenny Garment's politics.

segments.chapter: Venuti, Billie Rogers and Henry Jerome
segments.title: Jerome's experimental band and Mandel's early charts
segments.summary: The Jerome band is described as an early bop band; Mandel remembers his weak early charts and the surprise reunion for Henry Jerome.

segments.chapter: Venuti, Billie Rogers and Henry Jerome
segments.title: The lost draft card
segments.summary: Mandel says the draft board lost his registration and he never heard from them again.

segments.chapter: Boyd Raeburn and Jimmy Dorsey
segments.title: Joining Boyd Raeburn's band
segments.summary: In June 1945 Mandel joins Raeburn, calling it a roller-coaster ride, and describes players like Tommy Allison, Dale Pierce, Frank Socolow, Stu Anderson and George Handy.

segments.chapter: Boyd Raeburn and Jimmy Dorsey
segments.title: Raeburn, Auld and Rich as feeders for Woody Herman
segments.summary: Discussion of Serge Chaloff and of bands that served as farm teams for Herman, plus the great Washington players from Sonny Dunham's band.

segments.chapter: Boyd Raeburn and Jimmy Dorsey
segments.title: Leaving Raeburn for Jimmy Dorsey's band
segments.summary: Mandel left Raeburn near the end of 1945 for Jimmy Dorsey, finding it a stiff, unswinging band apart from its rhythm section, which became Soft Winds.

segments.chapter: Boyd Raeburn and Jimmy Dorsey
segments.title: Playing lead trombone and Ginnie Powell
segments.summary: Mandel says he followed Trummy Young and Tommy Pederson as lead trombonist in Raeburn's band on high chops, and mentions singer Ginnie Powell.

segments.chapter: Boyd Raeburn and Jimmy Dorsey
segments.title: The Raeburn book recovered
segments.summary: Mandel describes how little of his writing for Raeburn was recorded, and Kirchner explains how the Raeburn book was tracked down and played at a Smithsonian concert.

segments.chapter: Boyd Raeburn and Jimmy Dorsey
segments.title: George Williams charts credited to Mandel
segments.summary: He says many Raeburn arrangements credited to him were George Williams charts he disliked as vanilla and cluttered with sixteenth notes.

segments.chapter: Boyd Raeburn and Jimmy Dorsey
segments.title: George Handy's writing and the limits of the big band
segments.summary: Mandel explains what Handy taught him about orchestral color and doubles, and reflects that a big band is best as an instrument for swinging, with Ellington transcending its limits.

segments.chapter: Boyd Raeburn and Jimmy Dorsey
segments.title: Raeburn's band after Mandel left
segments.summary: After Mandel left, Raeburn reorganized in Los Angeles with Si Zentner, Johnny Richards and Handy's Dalvatore Sally, and the band folded in 1946.

segments.chapter: Boyd Raeburn and Jimmy Dorsey
segments.title: Johnny Richards's hard book and Mandel's reading
segments.summary: Mandel finds Richards technically brilliant but unfun to play, recalls failing a trumpet tryout, and discusses his reading versus Stan Getz and Joe Maini.

segments.chapter: Ellington, Basie and Lester Young
segments.title: Ellington's methods and unorthodox writing
segments.summary: Mandel calls Ellington and Basie his big influences and describes Ellington's secrecy, rule-breaking sketches and contrast with Strayhorn.

segments.chapter: Ellington, Basie and Lester Young
segments.title: Throwing Ko-Ko out the window
segments.summary: Mandel recalls hearing Ellington's Ko-Ko on a new 78 at school in 1941, hurling it into the snow in anger and buying another the next day.

segments.chapter: Ellington, Basie and Lester Young
segments.title: Never getting to know Ellington
segments.summary: Mandel says he never had contact with Ellington because of his shyness, and agrees the band was either wonderful or terrible, never mediocre.

segments.chapter: Ellington, Basie and Lester Young
segments.title: Basie and Lunceford as the real innovators
segments.summary: Mandel says Basie and Lunceford were the source of swing and the white bands pale imitations, though he praises Tommy Dorsey's Sy Oliver book with Buddy Rich.

segments.chapter: Ellington, Basie and Lester Young
segments.title: Hearing Basie and Lester Young in 1943
segments.summary: Mandel recalls hearing Basie live, then catching Lester Young just back in the band in 1943, and why Lester's soulful melodic playing declined after the Army.

segments.chapter: Ellington, Basie and Lester Young
segments.title: Lester Young's influences, disciples and Trumbauer
segments.summary: Discussion of Lester's alto beginnings, disciples such as Ammons, Dexter Gordon and Wardell Gray, his love of Frankie Trumbauer, and Goodman and Shaw as clarinetists.

segments.chapter: Ellington, Basie and Lester Young
segments.title: What Basie's band meant to Mandel
segments.summary: Mandel says Basie had a profound effect on him; he loved all the Basie bands, even the early head-arrangement ones.

segments.chapter: Ellington, Basie and Lester Young
segments.title: Orchestrating Lester Young
segments.summary: Mandel and Kirchner discuss trying to orchestrate Lester's solos for sections, the Bill Perkins octet record, and precursors of Supersax and the Prez Conference.

segments.chapter: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
segments.title: Buddy Rich's first band and Earl Swope
segments.summary: Mandel left Jimmy Dorsey for Buddy Rich's first band in 1946, a stiff band whose bright spot was trombonist Earl Swope, whom he compares to Carl Fontana.

segments.chapter: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
segments.title: Great trombonists: Harris, Nanton, Jenney, Teagarden
segments.summary: Mandel surveys trombone voices from Bill Harris and Lawrence Brown to Tricky Sam Nanton, Jack Jenney, Teagarden and Tommy Dorsey.

segments.chapter: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
segments.title: The Jimmy Dorsey trombone book and Bobby Byrne
segments.summary: Mandel describes the trombone chair in Jimmy Dorsey's band, written for Tommy-style players, and following Bobby Byrne and Moe Zudekoff.

segments.chapter: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
segments.title: Earl and Rob Swope and the Washington players
segments.summary: Mandel praises Earl Swope's time, says they became close, and talks about the Swope family and why the Washington musicians stayed home.

segments.chapter: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
segments.title: Buddy Rich's band personnel and later stints
segments.summary: Mandel names players in Buddy Rich's early band, says they hated each other at first but got along on later stints through 1948, then mentions Georgie Auld and Alvino Rey.

segments.chapter: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
segments.title: Writing The Song Is You for Buddy Rich
segments.summary: Mandel explains his experimental 1947 polyphonic arrangement, using contrasting mutes and woodwinds so each line can be heard, and the classical composers behind it.

segments.chapter: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
segments.title: Walking through Central Park and the modulations
segments.summary: Mandel recalls working out the ending while walking through Central Park, and Kirchner traces the chart's modulations.

segments.chapter: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
segments.title: What happened to the scores
segments.summary: They discuss how arrangers left scores with leaders, how copies of The Song Is You survived, and Buddy Rich keeping the charts by his bed.

segments.chapter: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
segments.title: Performing the chart: musical chairs for dancers
segments.summary: Mandel recalls Buddy Rich making players stand for entrances and the chart's stiff tempo for dancers.

segments.chapter: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
segments.title: Not remembering his own arrangements
segments.summary: Mandel says he often forgets what he wrote until he hears it played back, which feels as if he dreamt it.

segments.chapter: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
segments.title: Mandel's musical memory from childhood
segments.summary: He says he remembers arrangements and keys from 1927-28 heard as a toddler.

segments.chapter: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
segments.title: Manhattan School and the collapse of the big bands
segments.summary: Mandel decided to study after leaving Alvino Rey, as the big bands broke up in late 1946, and says one should learn jazz first.

segments.chapter: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
segments.title: Georgie Auld's band in 1946
segments.summary: Mandel found Georgie Auld's swinging band fun, with charts by Al Cohn, Manny Albam and others.

segments.chapter: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
segments.title: Alvino Rey's ten-brass band and George Handy's charts
segments.summary: Mandel joined Alvino Rey, playing bass trumpet in a huge brass section with George Handy writing atypical charts such as Stocking Horse.

segments.chapter: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
segments.title: Alvino Rey the inventor and eccentric
segments.summary: Mandel describes Rey as a six-foot-five Ohioan with novelty tastes, unicycle ambitions, the King Sisters and a flair for electronics.

segments.chapter: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
segments.title: Fighting his way into Manhattan School
segments.summary: Mandel studied counterpoint and fugue at Manhattan School after camping on its doorstep, with Dick Katz and Russ Savakus as fellow jazz students, and attended a Juilliard summer session.

segments.chapter: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
segments.title: Back with Buddy Rich and leaving for California
segments.summary: In fall 1947 Mandel returned to a changed Rich band, stayed until late 1948 and left in San Francisco to get his California union card.

segments.chapter: Gil Evans, Birth of the Cool and the Second Herd
segments.title: Missing Birth of the Cool and bass trumpet
segments.summary: Mandel says he would have been the trombonist on Birth of the Cool had he not gone to Los Angeles, and explains why he preferred bass trumpet.

segments.chapter: Gil Evans, Birth of the Cool and the Second Herd
segments.title: Bass trumpet versus valve trombone
segments.summary: Mandel says the bass trumpet is a resistant, unrewarding instrument compared to valve trombone or bass flugelhorn.

segments.chapter: Gil Evans, Birth of the Cool and the Second Herd
segments.title: Blossom Dearie brings him to Gil Evans
segments.summary: Mandel lived a block from Gil Evans without knowing it until Blossom Dearie told him to meet Gil; he recalls knowing Mulligan and the Georgie Auld small band.

segments.chapter: Gil Evans, Birth of the Cool and the Second Herd
segments.title: Writing across the orchestra
segments.summary: Mandel and Kirchner discuss his and Gil Evans's shared approach to orchestral color, Ellington's influence, impressionist composers and Gil's age.

segments.chapter: Gil Evans, Birth of the Cool and the Second Herd
segments.title: Gil's basement apartment and the Thornhill band
segments.summary: Mandel describes the basement apartment behind the Chinese laundry as a round-the-clock musical den, and Gil's Thornhill band and its players.

segments.chapter: Gil Evans, Birth of the Cool and the Second Herd
segments.title: Who came to Gil's and what it gave them
segments.summary: He names regulars like Mulligan, Savakus, John Lewis and George Russell, notes Charlie Parker visited but did not hang, and calls it a cross-pollination of ideas.

segments.chapter: Gil Evans, Birth of the Cool and the Second Herd
segments.title: Sonny Berman
segments.summary: Mandel remembers trumpeter Sonny Berman of Woody Herman's First Herd as a comic showman and the first of his crowd to die.

segments.chapter: Gil Evans, Birth of the Cool and the Second Herd
segments.title: Drugs and jazz
segments.summary: Mandel says he avoided hard drugs and argues that heroin was a plague on the music business from about 1943 for a decade, not typical of jazz.

segments.chapter: Gil Evans, Birth of the Cool and the Second Herd
segments.title: Getting a California union card
segments.summary: Mandel explains union residency rules in Los Angeles and New York, the six-month wait, and how he left the day he qualified.

segments.chapter: Gil Evans, Birth of the Cool and the Second Herd
segments.title: Back to New York with Chubby Jackson
segments.summary: In spring 1949 Mandel got a job in Chubby Jackson's swinging band at Bop City with Tiny Kahn.

segments.chapter: Gil Evans, Birth of the Cool and the Second Herd
segments.title: Writing Not Really the Blues for Woody Herman
segments.summary: While waiting for his card, Mandel wrote Not Really the Blues for the Second Herd, which Bill Harris avoided reading and the band later recorded.

segments.chapter: Gil Evans, Birth of the Cool and the Second Herd
segments.title: Carisi's Israel and Woody's taste
segments.summary: They discuss John Carisi's Israel, written first for Woody's band, which Mandel says did not suit Herman.

segments.chapter: Gil Evans, Birth of the Cool and the Second Herd
segments.title: Woody Herman, Eddie Sauter and experimental writers
segments.summary: Mandel contrasts Woody's tolerance for experiment with Artie Shaw and Benny Goodman's use of Eddie Sauter, and says he never got to know Sauter.

segments.chapter: Tiny Kahn, radio and Your Show of Shows
segments.title: Bill Holman's swinging lines
segments.summary: Mandel and Kirchner praise Bill Holman's linear unison writing, tracing it to Mulligan's charts for Kenton.

segments.chapter: Tiny Kahn, radio and Your Show of Shows
segments.title: Tiny Kahn, natural musician
segments.summary: Mandel describes Tiny Kahn as a self-taught, swinging drummer and writer, a close friend since 1945, with whom he shared a love of Basie.

segments.chapter: Tiny Kahn, radio and Your Show of Shows
segments.title: Writing and playing for Elliot Lawrence
segments.summary: Mandel, Cohn and Kahn wrote for and played in Elliot Lawrence's band, which Mandel says had a good conductor but no real rhythm section.

segments.chapter: Tiny Kahn, radio and Your Show of Shows
segments.title: Why big bands should keep a guitar
segments.summary: Mandel argues a good rhythm guitarist helps a band like Woody's or Terry Gibbs's Dream Band.

segments.chapter: Tiny Kahn, radio and Your Show of Shows
segments.title: The Second Herd as the best white band
segments.summary: Mandel calls Woody's Second Herd the best white band he knew, naming the brass and saxophones, and describes how Earl Swope led the section without trying.

segments.chapter: Tiny Kahn, radio and Your Show of Shows
segments.title: Stan Fishelson and hearing the Second Herd live
segments.summary: Mandel recalls meeting trumpeter Stan Fishelson in the Borscht Belt around 1941, praises his lead playing, and says Fishelson became a contractor.

segments.chapter: Tiny Kahn, radio and Your Show of Shows
segments.title: How Mandel, Cohn and Kahn worked together
segments.summary: The three arrangers played each other their charts at the piano; Mandel dates the Elliot Lawrence writing from 1952, after radio and television work.

segments.chapter: Tiny Kahn, radio and Your Show of Shows
segments.title: Playing with Stan Getz and Stan's first recordings of his music
segments.summary: After Chubby Jackson's band folded Mandel played trombone with Getz for several weeks, wrote charts such as Hershey Bar, and turned down staying on the road.

segments.chapter: Tiny Kahn, radio and Your Show of Shows
