segments.title: Staff arranger at WMGM radio
segments.summary: Mandel became a staff arranger at the WMGM radio station, brought in Billy Byers, and began writing strings and dramatic music for radio plays.

segments.chapter: Tiny Kahn, radio and Your Show of Shows
segments.title: Writing for Your Show of Shows
segments.summary: Mandel and Irwin Kostal supplied live weekly music for Sid Caesar's 90-minute show, an education in strings, dancers and visual cues.

segments.chapter: Tiny Kahn, radio and Your Show of Shows
segments.title: Sid Caesar the saxophonist and the timeline
segments.summary: Mandel notes that Caesar was a modest saxophonist who jammed with them, and dates the Show of Shows period to 1950-52.

segments.chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
segments.title: Joining Count Basie's band
segments.summary: Because Elliot Lawrence's band was not full-time, Mandel wrote for Basie and was called to join, replacing Jimmy Wilkins as second trombone.

segments.chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
segments.title: Meeting Basie as a cadet: it's the way we play it
segments.summary: Mandel recalls Earl Warren, Buddy Tate and Sweets taking him under their wing and Basie telling him it isn't the music but the way the band plays it.

segments.chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
segments.title: Dates with Basie and the unrecorded charts
segments.summary: They fix Mandel's Basie stay as June to November 1953; his chart Straight Life was recorded and he laments how little of his work was.

segments.chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
segments.title: What playing in Basie's band felt like
segments.summary: Mandel says Basie was the only band that felt inside as it sounded outside, praising the rhythm section and Basie's influence on Buddy Rich.

segments.chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
segments.title: Gus Johnson and the string of bass players
segments.summary: Mandel recalls Gene Ramey, Milt Hinton and Al Hall leaving, then Leroy Johnson on electric bass, until Eddie Jones stayed.

segments.chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
segments.title: Basie sax section, Neal Hefti and Ernie Wilkins
segments.summary: Mandel notes the Franks and Lockjaw joining, then praises arrangers Ernie Wilkins and Neal Hefti for easy-playing, swinging charts.

segments.chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
segments.title: The curved soprano saxophones in Elliot's band
segments.summary: Mandel says the curved soprano saxes in Elliot Lawrence's band were his idea, to get an older high saxophone-section sound.

segments.chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
segments.title: Artie Shaw's 1949 saxophone section
segments.summary: They name the saxophone section of Shaw's band, with Herbie Steward, Al Cohn, Socolow, Zoot Sims and Danny Bank.

segments.chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
segments.title: Artie Shaw's 1949 bebop band and its writers
segments.summary: Mandel says Shaw returned in 1949 wanting a bebop band, was open to change unlike Goodman, and used writers like George Russell, Gene Roland and Eddie Sauter.

segments.chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
segments.title: Mandel's charts for Shaw and Shaw's rewrite of piano parts
segments.summary: They identify Mandel's charts for Shaw on the 1989 CD, and Mandel says Shaw rewrote his piano passages for orchestra because of out-of-tune pianos.

segments.chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
segments.title: Shaw teaches arrangers; Shaw versus Goodman
segments.summary: Shaw taught Jerry Gray and Les Robinson what he wanted, and Mandel and Kirchner compare Shaw's intellect with Goodman's personality.

segments.chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
segments.title: Rehearsing Shaw's band in Buffalo and Cleveland-era band members
segments.summary: The band rehearsed under manager Lenny Lewis before Shaw arrived, with Porky Cohen, Sonny Russo, Fagerquist and Dale Pierce, but hit a terrible business time.

segments.chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
segments.title: The 1949 collapse of the bebop bands and Kenton's groups
segments.summary: They list the bands that folded in 1949, and Kenton's Innovations and later Holman-Rogers band, and the rhythm sections of pianist leaders.

segments.chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
segments.title: Guitar in big-band rhythm sections
segments.summary: They discuss why bandleaders dropped guitar, how chugging guitarists tied down rhythm sections, and the good players like Freddie Green and Barry Galbraith.

segments.chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
segments.title: The end of the big band era
segments.summary: Mandel says 1949 was a good time for music but a lousy time for bands, and that Elliot's band was a high-grade pickup band.

segments.chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
segments.title: Why Mandel wanted soprano saxophones
segments.summary: Mandel explains his tiredness with tenor-heavy sections, wanting second altos and curved sopranos, found in hockshops in 1952.

segments.chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
segments.title: Sidney Bechet and Johnny Hodges on soprano
segments.summary: Mandel talks about Bechet's vibrato and mastery, Early Hodges sounding like Bechet, and why Hodges gave up soprano in 1940.

segments.chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
segments.title: Clarinet versus soprano and Bechet's competitiveness
segments.summary: They debate whether Hodges played clarinet, compare clarinet and soprano, and note that Bechet used the soprano to dominate trumpet players.

segments.chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
segments.title: How the soprano experiment ended, and flutes and clarinets
segments.summary: The soprano idea lasted only a few tunes, and Mandel says flutes and clarinets were out of fashion but he used them for high sounds in The Song Is You.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Arriving in Los Angeles and string charts for Chet Baker
segments.summary: Mandel left Basie at the end of 1953, then wrote string charts for Chet Baker, disliking small string sections, with Dick Bock helping him find work.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Quitting Basie and choosing writing over playing
segments.summary: Mandel regrets leaving Basie but says writing kept pulling him from playing, so at about 29 he stopped; Billy Byers and Bob Brookmeyer kept both.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Al Cohn's career and Flo
segments.summary: Mandel explains why Al Cohn gave up writing to become a full-time saxophonist after losing sight in one eye, and mentions Flo, Ella Mae Morse's sister.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Chet Baker's records: Love, alto flute and Tommyhawk
segments.summary: They discuss the four string charts for Chet Baker, Mandel finishing the bridge of Love, Bud Shank's alto flute, and Chet recording Tommyhawk.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Chet Baker and Jack Sheldon
segments.summary: Mandel remembers Chet as a kid and natural, then working with Jack Sheldon, including The Sandpiper score where he wrote Miles on the trumpet part.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Jack Sheldon, Joe Mondragon and the gun
segments.summary: Mandel tells a story of Mondragon pulling a gun after Jack Sheldon was punched, and discusses Mondragon's Apache heritage and Miles Davis.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Missing the jazz fraternity and aging peers
segments.summary: Mandel says he moved north of Malibu in 1970 and misses the brotherhood of jazz musicians, and with Kirchner discusses Benny Carter's outliving contemporaries.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Stopping playing after the Haig with Zoot Sims
segments.summary: The last playing Mandel did was bass trumpet with Zoot Sims and Jimmy Rowles at the Haig, after which he put the horn down to become a full-time writer.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Opinion of West Coast jazz
segments.summary: Mandel says he never believed in West Coast jazz, which he finds weak next to hard-swinging Basie and East Coast players, and does not recall Chico Hamilton's offer.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Shelly Manne as a drummer
segments.summary: Mandel praises Shelly Manne as the tastiest, most sound-conscious small-band drummer but not a big-band drummer like Mel Lewis, Tiny Kahn or Buddy Rich.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Tiny Kahn, Mel Lewis and the role of taste
segments.summary: Mandel says Mel Lewis modeled himself on Tiny Kahn, and that taste, as with Basie and Sweets, is the arbiter of greatness; Manne's dynamics are admired.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Just a Child and other tunes recorded by others
segments.summary: Mandel recalls writing Just a Child for Bill Perkins's octet, Getz recording it later, Perkins's Mandel album around 1970, and Hal McKusick's Tommyhawk.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Production numbers for You're Never Too Young
segments.summary: Mandel did big dance numbers and Basie-like writing for a marching band in a Martin and Lewis film, thanks to Lou Brown, but does not count it as his first film.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Jerry Lewis's kindness to Frank Socolow
segments.summary: Kirchner and Mandel talk about Jerry Lewis paying hospital bills when Socolow's son was badly burned.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Studying with Stefan Wolpe
segments.summary: On the second day Mandel recalls a year or two of study with Wolpe around 1951, learning atonal writing, and says he learns better by experience than formal schooling.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: George Tremblay and atonal writing
segments.summary: Mandel praises George Tremblay, who taught many film writers a sensual Berg-like approach to atonality.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Jazz and Mulligan in I Want to Live!
segments.summary: Mandel explains the film's source music versus score, and that Gerry Mulligan appeared because the real Barbara Graham loved his music.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Instrumentation of the I Want to Live! score
segments.summary: Mandel says he chose his jazz orchestra with four French horns and unusual winds because they matched the sounds in his head, creating the first all-jazz film score.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Hollywood's reaction and Mancini's Peter Gunn
segments.summary: Mandel was passed over for an Oscar nomination because the old guard disliked jazz, while Mancini's Peter Gunn the same year helped crack the ice.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Not writing dark music
segments.summary: Mandel says he does not naturally write dark music and has stopped writing background music for violent scenes, and that he once disliked minor keys.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Percussion chase cue and the problem of telegraphing
segments.summary: Mandel describes the seven-minute percussion chase cue and his dislike of music that telegraphs what will happen on screen.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Backing into film scoring
segments.summary: Mandel says Jack Lewis got him the job, that he did not push for film work, and that doors only opened again in the early 1960s after B pictures.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Watching the film first
segments.summary: Mandel describes how he likes to watch a rough cut alone before discussing the score with the producer and director.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Spotting, the music editor and computing the cue
segments.summary: Mandel describes spotting sessions, working from the music editor's timed breakdown, plotting a climax backward from its hit point and conducting to picture.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Orchestration help under deadlines
segments.summary: Mandel explains that television deadlines force composers to bring in help for the mechanical work, and Kirchner notes Bill Holman orchestrated from his detailed sketches.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Hummers and writing his own orchestrations
segments.summary: Mandel defines Hummers, composers who cannot write music and hire orchestrators, and says he orchestrates everything himself because he hears it all in his head.

segments.chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
segments.title: Mancini, Hefti and J.J. Johnson's Across 110th Street
segments.summary: They discuss composers' use of orchestrators, and Kirchner notes J.J. Johnson's percussion cue echoed Mandel's I Want to Live! cue.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: Why Mandel disliked television writing
segments.summary: Mandel considers television inferior to film and the graveyard of composers like Duane Tatro and Earle Hagen, and they chat about Hagen's Harlem Nocturne.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: Ben Casey, Mister Roberts and the Andy Williams show
segments.summary: Mandel recalls TV episodes and the live Andy Williams variety show where he met Dave Grusin and joked with Williams's perfect ears.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: Motivic development and the twelve-tone Point Blank score
segments.summary: Mandel explains that he wrote Point Blank (1967) around a tone row and motif, as one of his favorite film projects.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: Vocal albums with David Allyn
segments.summary: Mandel describes how he and the singer chose tunes and budgets for albums such as David Allyn's all-Kern Sure Thing, made about 1957-58.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: Record companies and the lost tapes of the vaults
segments.summary: Mandel and Kirchner lament the shelved second Allyn album, praise CD reissues, and tell stories of record companies trashing old masters.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: Jo + Jazz with Ellington sidemen
segments.summary: For Jo Stafford's album Mandel used Ben Webster, Lawrence Brown, Harry Carney and Johnny Hodges while Ellington was on a European trip.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: Rabbit Hodges and great communicators
segments.summary: Mandel calls Johnny Hodges his favorite player and says Hodges, Getz, Lester Young, Parker and Louis had nothing between their thoughts and the listener.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: Irving Townsend's concept and Jo Stafford's choices
segments.summary: Mandel credits Columbia A&R man Irving Townsend with the concept for Jo + Jazz and says Jo chose the tunes, later reissued by Jo and Paul Weston.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: The Mel Tormé album with Ellington and Basie tunes
segments.summary: Mandel recalls the Tormé record on Duke and the Count, a collaboration that Mel called his favorite, with Mel giving a free hand.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: Ring-a-Ding-Ding! and Sinatra's arrangers and soloists
segments.summary: Mandel discusses writing Sinatra's first Reprise album, how his jazz-minded approach differed from Nelson Riddle and Billy May.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: Five- and six-way saxophone voicings and drop twos
segments.summary: Mandel explains his preference for five- and six-way saxophone voicings, using at least two altos, and compares his usage with Thad Jones's drop-two voicings.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: Bass saxophone and baritone setups
segments.summary: They compare Clare Fischer's sax section with bass saxophone and Kenton's two baritones, with Mandel saying the top baritone gets the part nobody wants.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: A flexible woodwind section with alto flutes and contrabass clarinet
segments.summary: Mandel explains his six-woodwind setup of two flutes, two alto flutes, bass clarinet and contrabass clarinet for flexibility.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: Why contrabass clarinet and low voices
segments.summary: Mandel praises the E-flat contrabass clarinet's range and says jazz bands lack bass and soprano voices.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: E-flat clarinet and low piccolo in I Want to Live!
segments.summary: Mandel explains the chilling E-flat clarinet and low-register piccolo in the gas chamber scene, and instruments played out of register, which the players liked.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: Joe Maini
segments.summary: Mandel calls Joe Maini the best lead alto he knew, a funny, Parker-influenced player who feigned ignorance but was intelligent.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: Lenny Bruce and the state of comedy
segments.summary: Mandel says Lenny Bruce was the most creative comic ever and that comedy now is stupid compared with the 1950s and 1960s.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: Knowing Lenny Bruce
segments.summary: Mandel recalls seeing Lenny Bruce work, his mother Sally Marr, his improvisation, and how his legal troubles ended his comedy.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: Maini in strip joints and the sound of I Want to Live!
segments.summary: Mandel says hearing Maini's raw alto in L.A. strip joints gave him the sound for the arrest scenes, since you had to outplay the drummer there.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: Using Joe Maini and Art Pepper
segments.summary: Mandel says he used Joe Maini on everything once he found him, and used Art Pepper on the Hoagy Carmichael album after playing with him in Latin bands in the late 1940s.

segments.chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
segments.title: Art Pepper, Chet Baker and the drug era
segments.summary: Mandel calls Art Pepper like a brother and a drug casualty like Chet, and they discuss the 1945-60 drug period alongside great music.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Ring-a-Ding-Ding! charts Mandel could not write himself
segments.summary: Mandel admits he farmed out parts of some Sinatra charts because he froze trying to get them perfect, and says Sinatra hired him after hearing his work for Vic Damone and David Allyn.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Working with Sinatra: credits and retakes
segments.summary: Mandel describes Sinatra crediting arrangers, hating rehearsals, and being made to redo a take after a trumpet clam, since he needs an audience to work to.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Streisand, Doris Day and singers' stage fright
segments.summary: They compare Sinatra's and Streisand's mental control, and Mandel recalls Doris Day, who eventually refused to sing with the band on record dates.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Mandel's favorite singers
segments.summary: Mandel prefers intimate singers such as Peggy Lee, Shirley Horn, Billie Holiday and Carmen McRae to belters, and says Sinatra has no peer.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Making Here's to Life with Shirley Horn
segments.summary: Mandel describes writing the orchestra around Shirley Horn's piano and voice tracks in 1990-91, and her firm ideas about chords.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: The Miles Davis album that never happened
segments.summary: Mandel recalls Miles Davis was meant to play on the Horn album and that they planned their own project near his death, which Miles shied from as a repeat of Gil Evans.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: The Americanization of Emily and the start of songwriting
segments.summary: After vocal albums and the Andy Williams show, Mandel got a Filmways picture that let him write his first song of consequence.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Mulligan's concert jazz band charts of I Want to Live! themes
segments.summary: Mandel wrote three charts of his I Want to Live! themes for Gerry Mulligan's concert jazz band, which Stan Getz later recorded.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Stan Getz's Voices album and vocal groups
segments.summary: Kirchner describes Getz's mid-60s album Voices, with a Claus Ogerman chorus, and Mandel recalls Blossom Dearie's skill at writing for voices.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Understated singers: Helen Merrill, Sade and others
segments.summary: Mandel admires understated singers like Helen Merrill, Jeri Southern and Julie London, and, among newer ones, Sade, Sheryl Crow and Diane Schuur.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: String albums of the 1950s: Dick Haymes and Michel Legrand
segments.summary: Mandel recalls Emily's string section and his 1955 Dick Haymes album, and praises Legrand's Paris albums as brilliantly orchestrated.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Robert Farnon, the master of string writing
segments.summary: Mandel calls Robert Farnon simply the best, the source of everything he stole, and also remembers Marion Evans, who left music.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Alex North and sensual writing
segments.summary: Mandel names Alex North and David Raksin as sensual writers and praises North's film scores, including Streetcar.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Scoring The Americanization of Emily and The Sandpiper
segments.summary: Mandel describes his first big MGM string section on Emily and the jazz-flavored Sandpiper score for Big Sur exteriors, with Jack Sheldon's trumpet.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: How The Shadow of Your Smile became a song
segments.summary: Mandel says the Sandpiper theme was demoed on piano before scoring and then turned into a song.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Paul Francis Webster and lyricists' credit
segments.summary: They discuss Webster's irate letter about credit for The Shadow of Your Smile and lyricists getting short shrift, from Hammerstein to Ira Gershwin and Mercer.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Winning the Oscar and its aftermath
segments.summary: Mandel describes Academy Award campaigning, winning in 1965, and the odd fact that the work dried up afterward.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: An American Dream and A Time for Love
segments.summary: Mandel recalls the violent Norman Mailer adaptation An American Dream, in which he placed the love song A Time for Love in a nightclub scene.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: The Russians Are Coming and the frightened chorus
segments.summary: Mandel describes scoring Norman Jewison's film with Hal Ashby editing and using nervous UCLA students to imitate a Red Army chorus.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: The Shining Sea and Peggy Lee's lyric
segments.summary: Mandel tells how Peggy Lee wrote a lyric that matched the screen action of The Russians Are Coming without knowing the scene.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Letting songs write themselves
segments.summary: Mandel says he lets songs write themselves, wrote The Shadow in about fifteen minutes in a restaurant, and prefers melody away from the piano rather than fitting a chord pattern.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Harper, Sure as You're Born and title songs
segments.summary: Mandel says Harper's theme became a song only because every film turned its theme into one, a practice he dates to High Noon and Laura.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Films after the Oscar: Pretty Poison and others
segments.summary: Mandel lists lesser pictures such as That Cold Day in the Park and Pretty Poison before MASH, noting the Oscar did not help his career.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Writing the MASH theme
segments.summary: Mandel tells how Altman's lyric, written by his teenage son, and a Leonard Cohen temp track led him to write Suicide Is Painless after some stiff drinks, and the lesson never to throw anything away.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Radio Tokyo speakers and the Japanese jazz records in MASH
segments.summary: Mandel recalls the awful 1949 Japanese jazz records that inspired the Radio Tokyo loudspeaker device, Altman's announcements, and cutting footage to music.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Favorite directors
segments.summary: Mandel names Altman, Hal Ashby, Sidney Lumet and John Boorman as directors he loved working with.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Faking terrible Japanese jazz records
segments.summary: Mandel says he duplicated the awful style rather than using real records, telling players to play their own style and sometimes writing in 6/8.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Agatha, Deathtrap and other films of the 1970s and 80s
segments.summary: Mandel recalls Summer Wishes, Winter Dreams, Agatha and Close Enough for Love, Staying Alive, Deathtrap with two harpsichords, and The Verdict.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Writing for voices in films
segments.summary: Mandel says he learned vocal writing by doing it and uses chorus only for a nationality or period, since voices pull the ear from dialogue.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: Rock soundtracks and the return of live orchestras
segments.summary: Mandel criticizes young filmmakers' rock soundtracks and welcomes the move from synthesizers back to live orchestra, as with French Kiss.

segments.chapter: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
segments.title: The shortage of big recording rooms
segments.summary: Mandel complains that large studios were torn down, so New York has few rooms for orchestras, and they discuss Astoria and Sony.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: Giving up film backgrounds
segments.summary: Mandel explains he stopped wanting to write film backgrounds through the 1970s and 80s, preferring records, and may do pops concerts.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: Henry Mancini and the limits of jazz scores
segments.summary: Mandel calls Mancini the ideal film and pops composer, and says jazz or rock scores each fit only a small fraction of movies.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: Arranging for Natalie Cole's Unforgettable
segments.summary: Mandel did about nine charts for Natalie Cole's Grammy-winning tribute to her father, with Bill Holman and Alan Broadbent also contributing.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: The Nat Cole duet idea and its influence
segments.summary: Mandel explains how Natalie's duet on Unforgettable began in clubs, why it worked only on that song, and how the album revived full-orchestra vocal records.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: The Manhattan Transfer Christmas album and Mandel's Christmas song
segments.summary: Mandel describes working with Manhattan Transfer and his song that came out sounding like Christmas, which the Bergmans confirmed.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: Becoming a record producer
segments.summary: Mandel says his producing career blossomed in the 1980s, when he could demand control as part of the arranging package, wanting to oversee a record from conception to mastering.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: Working with Michael Jackson
segments.summary: Mandel did large string arrangements for Michael Jackson's records, including Off the Wall and Dangerous, and calls him the most professional man in the studio.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: Using synthesizers within the orchestra
segments.summary: Mandel uses a DX7 and other synthesizers as hidden reinforcement of strings, and notes Jeremy Lubbock and David Foster do similar pop orchestration.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: Just a Child and writing songs as instrumentals
segments.summary: Mandel comments on his early songs like Just a Child, saying his generation wrote melodic themes as songs and he never wanted to be a Brill Building songwriter.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: Quietly There and Morgan Ames
segments.summary: Mandel says Quietly There was source music in Harper, with a later lyric by Morgan Ames, with whom he also wrote Unless It's You.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: Emily and the Singers Unlimited
segments.summary: Mandel explains Emily began as a motif for the Julie Andrews character, and remembers admiring Gene Puerling, with whom he worked on the Manhattan Transfer album.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: Instrumental titles: Groover Wailin' and El Cajon
segments.summary: Mandel explains the jokey titles of two instrumentals written for Cy Touff, Richie Kamuca and Al Cohn.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: Sure as You're Born and the Bergmans
segments.summary: Mandel recalls Alan and Marilyn Bergman writing a lyric for the Harper theme, praising their professionalism.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: Keester Parade and Something Different
segments.summary: Mandel jokes about the origins of Keester Parade and the deliberately stupid Something Different, which Bill Perkins recorded.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: Where Do You Start? and a playwright's lyric
segments.summary: Mandel describes how a playwright's divorce lyric inspired his music, which the Bergmans then matched with the same subject without knowing.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: You Are There and Dave Frishberg
segments.summary: Mandel says You Are There came to him one morning in the car and Dave Frishberg wrote the lyric after several attempts.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: I Wish I'd Met You and Richard Rodney Bennett
segments.summary: Mandel describes writing music to a lyric by Richard Rodney Bennett and Frank Underwood, and why he likes setting finished lyrics.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: Cinnamon and Clove, I Never Told You and Lena Horne's song
segments.summary: Mandel tells the origins of Cinnamon and Clove, I Never Told You from That Cold Day in the Park, and a recent song for Lena Horne.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: Joking about the eight-hour interview
segments.summary: After eight hours of interviewing Mandel jokes with Kirchner about hoping the tape is burned.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: Tribute albums and Tony Bennett's interest in his songs
segments.summary: Mandel talks about all-Mandel albums by Sue Raney, Bill Perkins and Fred Hersch, and Tony Bennett's wish to record more of his songs.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: The songbook and its piano tape
segments.summary: Mandel explains his Hal Leonard songbook, its cassette tutorial and the decline of music reading, with plans for an updated edition.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: Favorite songwriters
segments.summary: Asked for favorite songwriters, Mandel lists Berlin, Kern, Rodgers, Warren, Mercer and others, and mentions serving on the ASCAP board.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: Favorite film composers
segments.summary: Mandel names Alex North, Alfred Newman, Steiner, Raksin, Goldsmith, Mancini, Grusin and Bronislaw Kaper, and tells Kaper's joke about being a phony.

segments.chapter: Late career, producing and songwriting
segments.title: Closing reflections
segments.summary: Mandel closes by saying he is proud to be part of the American songwriting tradition and lucky to have spent his life doing what he loves.
